# Prospects for Inflation in a High Pressure Economy: Is the Phillips Curve Dead or Is It Just Hibernating? — Peter Hooper, Frederic S. Mishkin & Amir Sufi 2019

**Type:** paper
**Tags:** #phillips-curve #us-inflation #nairu #nonlinearity #inflation-expectations #wages #fed
**Source:** NBER Working Paper No. 25792 (May 2019), prepared for the 2019 US Monetary Policy Forum
**Language:** English
**Source file:** [[external/clean_md/us_inflation_phillips_curve (Hooper, Mishkin & Sufi, 2019)]]

---

## Context and motivation

From March 2017 US unemployment ran below the CBO's and the FOMC's estimates of the natural rate, and from March 2018 below 4%, levels last seen in the late 1960s, while core inflation stayed below the 2% objective. The FOMC had just pivoted to a "patient", essentially neutral stance. The flatness of the Phillips curve — rolling 20-year regressions show the slope on the unemployment gap collapsing from windows starting in the early 1980s, and near zero since the early 2000s — was being read as license to run a high-pressure economy with little inflation risk. The paper asks whether the curve is dead or "just hibernating", i.e. whether the flatness is a structural fact or an artefact of the data and of policy that could reverse in a tight labor market.

## Core argument / thesis

The price Phillips curve looks dead in national data since the late 1980s, but three features of that period, all products of successful monetary policy, make the estimate unreliable: (1) very few episodes of a tight labor market, so a slope that steepens only when unemployment is well below the natural rate cannot be detected; (2) policy endogeneity — a central bank that leans against overheating removes the correlation between slack and inflation, biasing the estimated slope toward zero; (3) anchored inflation expectations, which make inflation less persistent and the curve flatter for as long as the anchor holds. Data that escape the first two problems — states and metropolitan areas, where monetary policy is common and exogenous and tight labor markets are frequent — show a steep, nonlinear price curve; the wage Phillips curve remains steep and nonlinear even in national data. The 1960s show how an anchored, flat regime can shift to an unanchored one. Hence "reports of the death of the Phillips curve may be greatly exaggerated": the flatness reflects policy, and "A departure from this policy would likely lead to a steepening of the Phillips curve."

## Key mechanisms / model

**The equation.** A "plain vanilla" expectations-augmented Phillips curve, close to Yellen (2017) and Powell (2018a), deliberately not a New Keynesian curve with marginal cost: quarterly annualized core PCE inflation on a constant, the unemployment gap (U-3 minus the CBO natural rate), long-run inflation expectations (the FRB/US series: SPF ten-year expectations from 1981, a term-structure measure before, a moving average of inflation before 1967), seven lags of inflation, the change in relative import prices, and a dummy for the Nixon controls. The coefficients on expectations and lagged inflation are constrained to sum to one (price homogeneity). The wage curve replaces the dependent variable with wage growth (several measures) and adds HP-filtered trend productivity, with lagged *price* inflation — a real-wage Phillips curve.

**How slope and persistence combine.** The short-run slope is the gap coefficient. Persistence is the sum of the lagged-inflation coefficients; with the constraint, the longer-term slope equals the short-run slope divided by the weight on expectations (footnote 2). When the lags sum to one and expectations get no weight, the model is the accelerationist curve: a negative gap raises inflation until the gap closes. When the weight shifts to expectations, the same short-run slope produces a much smaller cumulative effect — "reduced inflation persistence effectively reduces the longer-term slope."

**Nonlinearity.** Five alternatives to the linear gap: a spline (different slopes for negative and positive gaps), a cubic in the gap, two convex forms (gap over unemployment; log of unemployment over the natural rate), and a one-sided piecewise quadratic that steepens only in tight markets (after Nalewaik). The question is whether the slope steepens as unemployment falls well below the natural rate.

**Why the national estimate can be biased toward zero** (Fitzgerald & Nicolini; McLeay & Tenreyro): a central bank minimizing inflation and output-gap deviations tightens when the gap is negative; in the limit optimal policy eliminates any observed correlation between inflation and slack. The estimated flattening then measures how responsive policy has been, not how inflation would respond if policy were passive.

**Why regional data identify it.** State and MSA regressions include year fixed effects, which remove all national variation (including monetary policy, common to all areas) and use within-area deviations of unemployment from the area's own average; area fixed effects absorb differences in natural rates. Theory would predict a *flatter* curve in MSAs, since goods trade across MSAs, so a steeper one is informative.

**Regime shift.** Following Nalewaik's Markov-switching model, the economy can move from a stationary regime (anchored expectations, transitory shocks, flat curve) to a nonstationary one (adaptive expectations, persistent shocks, steep curve) when a large and persistent negative gap raises actual inflation. The 1960s are the case study: inflation stayed around 1.5% while the gap fell toward -2, then took off in 1966 as unemployment fell below 4%, driven by fiscal expansion (Vietnam, Great Society, Medicare and Medicaid, with health-care prices leading), a Fed whose hikes left real rates little changed and which reversed them in early 1967, political pressure to coordinate with fiscal policy, and a misperceived natural rate.

## Main results / findings

- **National price curve, full sample.** Core PCE, 1961–2018: the linear slope is small (-0.141, Table 2.1), but strongly nonlinear — the spline slope is -0.423 when the gap is negative and close to zero (-0.048) when positive, and all nonlinear forms steepen further at a gap of -2. Extending headline PCE back to 1954 strengthens this; back to 1949 the slope flattens, possibly because the Korean War controls are not well handled.
- **National price curve, since 1988.** Core PCE, 1988–2018: the linear slope moves to -0.037 and none of the nonlinear terms is significant (Table 2.5); the linear model fits as well as the nonlinear ones. Persistence roughly halves (sum of lags 0.807 in Table 2.1 vs. 0.474 in Table 2.5) while the weight on expectations rises commensurately.
- **National wage curve.** Average hourly earnings, 1988–2018: the linear slope stays significant (-0.180) and the spline slope in tight markets is -0.929 (Table 2.6); other wage measures give similar results (Table 2.7). Rolling regressions show the wage slope and persistence falling much less than the price ones. Expectations become far more important for wages after 1988.
- **Lack of variation.** In the past three decades the unemployment gap was wider than -1 about 4% of the time, more than three times less often than over the full sample since 1962; only six quarters in 1999–2000 had a gap beyond -1 percentage point.
- **Regional curves.** MSA core CPI, 1990–2017: slope -0.301 with lagged MSA inflation (Table 3.2), and about -0.70 where unemployment is below 4%, flattening above 5.5%. State wages, 1981–2017: slope -0.41 (Table 3.1), about -0.99 below 4% unemployment, flatter above 7.5%. Collapsing the MSA data to one national series gives a much flatter -0.09, so the steeper regional slope comes from within-area variation, not from sample composition. Regional and national wage curves are similar; regional and national price curves are not.
- **Global factors.** Global output gaps and trade intensity are at best marginally significant or carry the wrong sign, and barely move the slope; the paper finds "little support for global factors explaining the flattening."
- **Scenarios (partial equilibrium, no policy reaction).** With full-sample coefficients, the FOMC's December 2018 unemployment path produces a rising inflation path, steeper in the nonlinear variants; post-1988 coefficients give paths close to the FOMC's. If unemployment falls to 3% and expectations become adaptive (an equation estimated on 1964Q1–1981Q4), inflation could rise to between 2.75% (linear) and 4.25% (spline) within three years; the wage projections tilt up much less, because lagged price inflation is held at the FOMC path.
- **What the evidence does not say.** The authors are explicit that it does not predict a rise in inflation: the pre- and post-1988 samples disagree, and the claim is only that complacency is not warranted.

## Limitations and caveats

- The case rests on choosing which sample to trust: the authors are "more doubtful" of the post-1988 estimates for the reasons above, but state that "We are not sure which Phillips curve sample periods provides more reliable information".
- Regional estimates identify a different object: with year fixed effects there is "no reason to expect similarity" with national coefficients, and the authors concede that regional Phillips curves are "less well grounded in theory". The national tight-market threshold (the CBO natural rate) and the regional one (4% unemployment) are not the same thing.
- The curve depends on the CBO natural rate and on the spliced FRB/US expectations series; neither is tested against alternatives in the text, and the 1960s episode itself shows how far a real-time natural rate can be from a later estimate (Romer & Romer put the Greenbook's implicit natural rate around 2.5%, against the CBO's 5.5%).
- The projections are "partial-equilibrium scenarios designed to show the properties of the different models rather than true forecasts" and ignore the policy reaction; the authors expect the Fed would step in.
- The gap between the steep wage curve and the flat price curve — a possibly weakened link from wages to prices — is left as a puzzle "for future research".
- Damaged passages: the two Phillips-curve equations in Section 2.2 and the adaptive-expectations equation in Section 5.1 have their subscripts and summation signs replaced by glyph codes; the coefficients survive in the text but the lag structure of the Section 5.1 equation cannot be read reliably. The definitions of the spline and piecewise-quadratic indicator variables are partly garbled (the latter is stated with the same condition, u > u*, as the former). Most figures survive as titles only, a few as axis numbers.
- Inconsistencies in the text: the literature review says Nalewaik's 1970s–early 1990s conformed "more to the stationary regime", which contradicts the surrounding argument; Section 5 cites a "Figure 5.15" that does not exist (the figures end at 5.10); Annex Tables A.1 and A.2 print an RMSE of 0.000 for some columns; Table 3.3 prints a positive tight-market slope (0.85) for compensation per hour 1964–2018 where the corresponding Annex Table A.3 value is negative, and its footnote defines a tight regional market as unemployment below 7% while the text uses 4%. The reference list is not in the file (the page numbering jumps from 54 to 58).

## Connections

- [[phillips_curve]] — the paper's object: the reduced-form expectations-augmented curve, its slope, persistence, nonlinearity, and why the national estimate flattened
- [[natural_rate_of_unemployment]] — slack is measured against the CBO natural rate; the 1960s Fed's misperceived natural rate as a cause of the Great Inflation
- [[inflation_persistence]] — the sum of lagged-inflation coefficients, halved after 1988, is what turns a short-run slope into a small long-run effect
- [[inflation_targeting]] — anchored expectations, helped by the Fed's 2012 explicit 2% objective, as the leading explanation of the flattening and the condition under which the curve stays asleep
- [[monetary_policy/synthesis/the_role_monetary_policy (Friedman, 1968)]] — the accelerationist limit of the paper's equation, and the 1960s as the episode where the trade-off broke down
- [[monetary_policy/synthesis/policy_rules_real_time_data (Orphanides, 2001)]] — the real-time measurement problem behind the 1960s error the paper describes: slack misjudged when policy was set
- [[verde_mp_mental_models]] — §3.2 (central banks "behind the curve" after an inflation shock): the paper's 1960s Fed is the historical case of the same failure
